title: Succession Without a Will Under Hindu Law: Heirs, Coparcenary and the Vineeta Sharma and Arunachala Gounder Rulings
subtitle: Whether a Hindu family's property passes by survivorship or by inheritance, and who counts as an heir, turns on a distinction the Hindu Succession Act draws but families routinely miss: whether the property was ancestral or self-acquired.
meta_description: How intestate succession works under Hindu law: Class I and II heirs, daughters' coparcenary rights, self-acquired property, and the documents heirs need.
author: Bhaskar Subramanian
standfirst: Most Hindu families who lose the head of the household without a will assume the law has one simple answer: the children inherit, perhaps with the widow, and that is that. The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 does produce a workable answer, but it does not produce a single one. A man's property is treated differently depending on whether it came to him as ancestral coparcenary property or as something he acquired himself, a woman's property is treated differently again depending on where it came from, and two Supreme Court decisions of the last few years, Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma and Arunachala Gounder v Ponnusamy, have settled questions that litigators spent over a decade arguing in High Courts across the country. This piece sets out how intestate succession actually works under Hindu law today, where mutation and legal heir certificates fit into the picture, and how the position compares with other personal laws.
key_points: A male Hindu's property devolves differently depending on its character. Separate or self-acquired property passes by inheritance under Section 8 to Class I heirs first; undivided coparcenary interest in joint family property, since the 2005 amendment, also devolves by succession rather than survivorship when he leaves a Class I female heir or a male heir claiming through such a female.

Class I heirs, the widow, sons, daughters, mother and certain heirs of predeceased children, take simultaneously and to the exclusion of every later class; only if no Class I heir exists does the estate move to Class II, then to agnates, then to cognates.

Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma, (2020) 9 SCC 1, held that a daughter becomes a coparcener by birth, so the 2005 amendment to Section 6 applies to every living daughter regardless of her date of birth, overruling the contrary view in Prakash v Phulavati and Mangammal v T.B. Raju.

Arunachala Gounder (Dead) by LRs v Ponnusamy, decided 20 January 2022, held that the self-acquired property of a Hindu male who died intestate, even before the 1956 Act came into force, devolves on his daughter by inheritance rather than passing by survivorship to male coparceners, under the old Hindu law principles the 1956 Act preserved.

A female Hindu's intestate property does not follow one single order of heirs. Section 15 sends her self-acquired property down the general order in Section 15(1), but property she inherited from her parents or her husband is pulled back to the source under Section 15(2) if she dies without children, so it goes to her parents' heirs or her husband's heirs rather than to her own general heirs.

A legal heir certificate, issued by a revenue officer such as a Tehsildar, identifies heirs for local, administrative purposes and is not a substitute for a succession certificate, which a civil court issues under the Indian Succession Act, 1925 to let an heir deal with the deceased's debts and securities; neither is proof of title to immovable property, and mutation in revenue records is weaker still.

Muslim, Christian and Parsi intestate succession each follow a materially different scheme from Hindu law, Muslim law applying fixed Quranic shares rather than a schedule of classes, and the Indian Succession Act, 1925 governing Christians and Parsis along different lines again, so a family with mixed personal-law heirs cannot simply apply Hindu succession rules by analogy.

sections.heading: Why the question is not as simple as "who are the heirs"
paragraphs: A death in a Hindu family without a will usually produces an immediate, practical question from the surviving relatives: who gets what. The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 answers that question, but it answers a prior question first, one families rarely think to ask before a dispute forces it on them. The prior question is what kind of property is actually on the table. Property a man held as his undivided interest in a Hindu Undivided Family, land or a house that came down through generations and was never partitioned, is treated by the Act very differently from a flat he bought with his own salary or a fixed deposit he built up over a career. Get that classification wrong and every later step, who counts as an heir, in what share, and whether a daughter's claim survives her father's death, can come out wrong as well.

The Act applies to anyone who is a Hindu by religion in any of its forms, which for this purpose includes Virashaivas, Lingayats, followers of the Brahmo, Prarthana or Arya Samaj, and also Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs by domicile, as Section 2 makes clear. It does not apply to Muslims, Christians, Parsis or Jews, each of whom has a separate intestate succession regime discussed later in this piece. Within that broad Hindu umbrella, the Act does not distinguish by caste or sect for purposes of who inherits, though regional custom occasionally surfaces in disputes over whether a particular family arrangement should be read as a will substitute or as something else entirely.

Two Supreme Court decisions anchor almost every live dispute a litigator sees today on this subject. Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma settled, after more than a decade of conflicting High Court and even Supreme Court authority, exactly which daughters become coparceners and from when. Arunachala Gounder v Ponnusamy settled a related but distinct question, how a man's self-acquired property, as opposed to his coparcenary share, passes to his daughter when he dies intestate. Both decisions matter because they correct assumptions that were common in practice for years, and a family relying on outdated advice from before 2020 or 2022 may well be acting on a position the Supreme Court has since reversed.

sections.heading: Coparcenary property and separate property: the distinction that drives everything else
paragraphs: Hindu law has long recognised two broad categories of property within a joint family. Coparcenary property, sometimes called ancestral property in loose usage, is property in which a coparcener acquires an interest by birth, classically property inherited up to four generations of male lineal descendants without having been partitioned. Before 2005, only sons, grandsons and great-grandsons were coparceners by birth; a coparcener's interest in this property did not pass by inheritance at all when he died, it passed by survivorship to the remaining coparceners, shrinking the pool of owners rather than adding new heirs.

Separate or self-acquired property is everything else a person builds up on their own, whether through salary, a business, a gift from someone other than the joint family, or a purchase funded independently of joint family funds. This property was always governed by the ordinary rules of inheritance in Section 8 of the Act, not by survivorship, which meant a man's widow, daughters and sons always had a claim to it on his death, independent of whatever coparcenary rules applied to the family's ancestral land.

The Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 changed the coparcenary side of this picture in a way that matters for every intestate succession worked out since. It amended Section 6 to make a daughter a coparcener by birth in her own right, with the same rights and liabilities as a son, and it abolished survivorship for coparcenary property where the deceased leaves a female Class I heir, or a male heir claiming through a female Class I heir, in which case the interest instead devolves by testamentary or intestate succession under the Act rather than passing automatically to the surviving coparceners. Where no such heir survives, survivorship among the remaining coparceners can still operate for what is left of the joint family's undivided property. Getting these two tracks, coparcenary succession versus survivorship, and separate property succession, confused is the single most common analytical error in intestate disputes within Hindu families.

sections.heading: A male Hindu dies intestate: the Section 8 hierarchy
paragraphs: Section 8 sets out the general order of succession to the property of a male Hindu who dies without a will, whether that property is his separate property or his coparcenary interest as devolved under the amended Section 6. The order runs in four tiers, and each tier is exhausted before the next is even considered: first the heirs specified in Class I of the Schedule to the Act, then, failing any Class I heir, the heirs specified in Class II, then the deceased's agnates, relatives connected wholly through males, and finally his cognates, relatives connected through one or more females in the chain.

Class I is deliberately broad and includes, among others, the widow, sons and daughters, the mother, and the heirs of a predeceased son or daughter, including sons and daughters of a predeceased son of a predeceased son. If even one Class I heir survives the deceased, the estate is distributed among the Class I heirs and the matter ends there; Class II heirs, who include the father, siblings and various more distant relatives arranged in nine further entries, inherit only when no Class I heir exists at all. Agnates and cognates come into the picture only on the rare occasion that neither class has a surviving member, which in most ordinary families, where a widow, a child or a grandchild through a predeceased child nearly always survives, is an unlikely scenario.

This tiered, winner-take-all structure within each class is worth stating plainly because families sometimes assume inheritance works on a sliding scale of closeness, with a surviving parent or sibling getting something even where children exist. Under Section 8, that is not the rule. A single surviving daughter excludes a surviving father, a surviving brother and every other Class II relative entirely, regardless of how close that relationship might otherwise seem.

Class I status does not depend on how a child came into the family. A child validly adopted under the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 ranks as a natural-born child of the adoptive parent for every purpose of inheritance from that parent, including as a Class I heir, while simultaneously losing any inheritance right in the family of their birth from the date of adoption. A child born of a marriage later held void or voidable is also treated, by a specific provision of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, as legitimate for purposes of inheriting from the parents, though not as conferring any claim on a wider joint family's coparcenary property beyond what that provision allows. Class II, by contrast, is organised as nine separate entries rather than one combined group, running from the father, through various combinations of siblings and their children, to more distant relatives such as a paternal grandfather's siblings; an heir in an earlier entry excludes an heir in a later one, so the structure within Class II repeats, on a smaller scale, the same winner-take-all logic that governs the relationship between Class I and Class II as a whole.

sections.heading: How Class I shares are actually divided: Section 10
paragraphs: Section 10 governs how the estate is split once the Class I heirs are identified, and it works on a branch basis rather than treating every living relative as an equal claimant from the outset. The widow takes one share. Each surviving child, son or daughter, takes one share. Where a child predeceased the intestate but left children of their own, those grandchildren together take the one share their deceased parent would have taken, dividing it equally among themselves rather than each taking a full share in their own right.

A short example makes the branch structure concrete. Suppose a man dies intestate leaving a widow, one surviving son, and the two children of a daughter who predeceased him. The estate splits into three equal shares at the first level: one to the widow, one to the son, and one to the predeceased daughter's branch. That third share is then divided equally between her two children, so each grandchild takes one half of that one-third share, or one-sixth of the whole, while the son takes a full third and the widow takes a full third. The branch rule prevents the accident of a parent's early death from either enlarging or shrinking what that parent's own children receive, in the end, relative to their uncles, aunts or grandmother, at least at the level the Act fixes for the branch as a whole.

One further point is worth flagging because it surprises families more often than the branch rule itself: a widow's share, once it vests on her husband's death, is not taken away by her remarrying afterwards. Older case law under the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act, 1856 had treated remarriage as a forfeiting event in some contexts, but the 1956 Act's scheme of succession does not import that consequence, and a widow's Class I share stands on the same footing as a son's or a daughter's once it has devolved on her, regardless of what she does with her life afterward. Where a dispute does arise over a widow's share, it is almost always a dispute about whether she was in fact validly married to the deceased, not about anything she did after his death.

sections.heading: Vineeta Sharma: why every living daughter is now a coparcener, regardless of her date of birth
paragraphs: The 2005 amendment to Section 6 was clear that daughters would be coparceners going forward, but it left open a question that produced years of conflicting decisions: did the amendment benefit only daughters born after 9 September 2005, when it took effect, or did it also benefit daughters who were already alive, even already adults, on that date, and what about daughters whose father had already died before the amendment came into force at all. In Prakash v Phulavati, decided in 2015, the Supreme Court had held that the amended Section 6 would apply only where the father, the coparcener through whom the daughter claimed, was himself alive on 9 September 2005. Mangammal v T.B. Raju took a broadly similar line shortly after.

Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma, decided by a three-judge bench on 11 August 2020 and reported at (2020) 9 SCC 1, overruled both of those decisions. The Court's reasoning rested on the basic nature of a coparcenary interest: it is acquired by birth, not by any subsequent event, and the 2005 amendment simply extends that birth-based rule to daughters in the same terms it had always applied to sons. On that logic, it makes no difference whether the daughter was born before or after September 2005, and it makes no difference whether her father died before that date either, so long as the succession to the coparcenary property in question had not already been finally concluded, for instance through a registered partition or a court decree, before the amendment took effect. Commentators have described the resulting position as retroactive rather than strictly retrospective, since the amendment operates on a status, coparcener by birth, that existed in substance before 2005 even though the statute recognising it for daughters only arrived that year.

The practical consequence for a litigator handling an intestate succession today is straightforward to state even where the facts are not: a daughter's claim to a share of coparcenary property cannot be defeated merely by showing that she was born, or that her father died, before 2005. What can still defeat it, consistent with the Court's own qualification in Vineeta Sharma, is proof that the coparcenary property was already finally partitioned by a registered instrument or a decree of a court before 20 December 2004, the date the amending Bill was introduced, a cutoff the judgment adopted to prevent reopening partitions long since settled on the law as it then stood.

sections.heading: Arunachala Gounder: self-acquired property follows inheritance, not survivorship, even for deaths before 1956
paragraphs: Vineeta Sharma dealt with coparcenary property. A separate and older line of difficulty concerned a man's self-acquired property, particularly where he had died before the 1956 Act existed at all, governed instead by the Hindu law as it stood under the Mitakshara school or by the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 where applicable. In Arunachala Gounder (Dead) by LRs v Ponnusamy, decided on 20 January 2022, the dispute concerned property one Marappa Gounder had purchased at a court auction in 1938, treated by the Supreme Court as his self-acquired property rather than ancestral joint family property. He died intestate, long before 1956, leaving an only daughter, Kuppayee Ammal.

The question was whether that self-acquired property passed to the daughter by inheritance, giving her an absolute and heritable interest of her own, or whether it instead passed by survivorship to the male members of the wider joint family, leaving the daughter with nothing beyond, at most, a right of maintenance. The Supreme Court held that self-acquired property of a Hindu male dying intestate has never, even under the old Mitakshara law the 1956 Act displaced, passed by survivorship; it devolves by inheritance to the deceased's heirs, and where he leaves a sole surviving daughter and no son, she takes it absolutely rather than merely holding a limited interest in it. The Court's reading of Section 15 of the 1956 Act, dealing with a female Hindu's own succession, reinforced this by treating sub-section (2)'s source-based exceptions as narrowly confined to inherited property, leaving self-acquired property to follow the general, broader order set out in sub-section (1).

The effect of Arunachala Gounder is to close a gap that families with older, pre-1956 deaths in their chain of title had sometimes exploited, or stumbled into without realising it: an assumption that a daughter of a man who died before the Act came into force could never have inherited his self-acquired property at all, so that any sale, partition or mutation treating only the sons or male collaterals as owners was safe from challenge. After this decision, that assumption no longer holds, and a title search touching property with a pre-1956 death in the chain should specifically ask whether a daughter's inheritance claim through that death was ever formally extinguished, rather than simply assuming it lapsed with time.

Arunachala Gounder also sits alongside Section 14 of the 1956 Act, which converts a Hindu woman's pre-existing limited estate, the kind of restricted interest a widow often held under the old law, into a full and absolute interest from the date the Act commenced, provided she was actually in possession of the property at that time. The two provisions do different jobs: Section 14 upgrades an interest a woman already held in some form, while the Arunachala Gounder line of authority decides whether a deceased man's self-acquired property passes to his daughter by inheritance in the first place. A practitioner tracing title through an estate with a death before 1956 should check both questions separately, since a family's own account of "what grandmother always told us" about who owned what often conflates the two and gets at least one of them wrong.

sections.heading: When a woman dies intestate: Sections 15 and 16, and why the source of the property matters
paragraphs: A female Hindu's intestate succession does not mirror a male's. Section 15(1) sets out a general order, sons and daughters (including children of a predeceased child) and the husband together first, then the husband's heirs, then the woman's own mother and father, then her father's heirs, and finally her mother's heirs. On its face this looks like a single ranked list similar to Section 8, and for the common case of a woman survived by children or a husband, it operates much like one.

Section 15(2) carves out two specific situations where the general order in sub-section (1) does not apply, and both turn on where the property came from rather than on who the woman's closest relatives happen to be. Where she dies without any son or daughter, or child of a predeceased child, and the property in question is something she herself inherited from her father or mother, that property does not go down the general Section 15(1) order at all; it reverts instead to the heirs of her father, effectively treating the property as though it had never left the paternal side of the family. Where, in the same childless situation, the property is something she inherited from her husband or from her father-in-law, it reverts correspondingly to the heirs of her husband. Property she acquired herself, by her own earnings, a gift unconnected to inheritance, or a purchase, is not pulled back to any source in this way and simply follows the general order in sub-section (1).

Section 16 then supplies the detailed rules for dividing property among whichever set of heirs Section 15 identifies, broadly preferring heirs who appear earlier in the relevant list over those who appear later, with heirs within the same entry sharing equally, including, on the authority relied on in later High Court decisions, sons and daughters taking simultaneously in equal shares rather than one class being preferred over the other. A woman's estate planning, where she wants her self-earned property to go somewhere other than this statutory order, including to relatives on her husband's side she is close to despite having no children, is one of the more common reasons advocates advise even modest estates to execute a will rather than leave the position to these source-tracing default rules.

sections.heading: Mutation, legal heir certificates and succession certificates: three different documents for three different jobs
paragraphs: Families dealing with an intestate estate commonly reach first for mutation, the revenue or municipal record reflecting whose name a property stands in for tax and local administrative purposes. Mutation matters practically, since it determines who the authorities will treat as liable for property tax and whom they will deal with for permissions, but it is not proof of title and does not itself transfer or confirm ownership. Courts have repeatedly held that a disputed question of inheritance cannot be resolved by a revenue officer's mutation entry; where title is genuinely contested, a civil suit for declaration and, if necessary, partition remains the forum that actually decides ownership.

A legal heir certificate performs a narrower, more local function. It is issued by a revenue authority, commonly a Tehsildar, Taluk office or Sub-Divisional Magistrate depending on the state, and it identifies who the deceased's heirs are for administrative purposes such as transferring a ration card, a pension, certain small bank balances, or employment dues. Because there is no single central statute governing it, the exact procedure, required documents and processing time vary from state to state, and a certificate issued in one state has no automatic standing to be relied upon in another for the same purpose.

A succession certificate is a different instrument altogether, issued under Part X of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 by a District Judge, on a petition under Section 372 naming all persons claiming to be entitled to succeed to the deceased's debts and securities. It establishes who may collect the deceased's movable financial assets, bank balances, shares, insurance proceeds and similar debts and securities, and most banks and financial institutions insist on one before releasing anything beyond fairly small sums. It does not, by itself, confer or prove title to immovable property, and a certificate holder who turns out not to be the rightful heir remains personally accountable to whoever is. Courts have held that payment of the court fee, usually calculated as a percentage of the value of the assets and payable before the certificate issues, can in appropriate circumstances be deferred to the point of issuance rather than at the filing stage, though the fee itself, and whether any state-specific exemption applies, for instance for a widow in certain circumstances, should be checked locally before filing.

In practice, a bank, housing society or sub-registrar dealing with an estate frequently asks for something beyond any of these three documents: a no-objection letter or indemnity from the other heirs, confirming that the heir seeking to deal with a specific asset is not acting against the interests of, or without the knowledge of, the rest. This is a matter of institutional risk management rather than a statutory requirement, and its absence does not by itself defeat an heir's underlying legal entitlement, but a family that can produce one, typically a short, simple document signed by all adult heirs, usually finds transfers and withdrawals go through considerably faster than a family that cannot or will not. States have also been progressively digitising land records and linking them to Aadhaar-based identity verification for mutation applications, which has sped up processing in many districts but has not changed the underlying legal position that a mutation entry, digital or paper, remains an administrative record rather than proof of ownership.

sections.heading: A short contrast with other personal laws
paragraphs: A family with members governed by different personal laws, common enough in cases involving conversion, inter-faith marriage, or simply a diverse set of relatives, cannot extend Hindu succession reasoning to a non-Hindu relative's estate by analogy. Muslim personal law does not use a schedule of classes at all; it applies fixed Quranic shares to specified relatives, with the precise shares differing between Sunni and Shia law and the two schools disagreeing in places on who qualifies as a sharer, a residuary or a distant kindred. A surviving spouse, children and parents typically all take a defined fractional share simultaneously rather than one class excluding another entirely, a structural difference from the Hindu Class I and II scheme that trips up practitioners trained primarily in Hindu succession law.

Christians and Parsis in India are governed by the Indian Succession Act, 1925, but under provisions distinct from the rules discussed in this piece, which concern Hindus specifically. The 1925 Act's intestate succession provisions for Christians, in Part V, follow their own order among a widow or widower, children and kindred, with shares calculated differently from either the Hindu or the Muslim scheme, and Parsis follow a further, separately structured set of rules within the same Act. A family dealing with an estate that includes relatives governed by more than one of these regimes, for instance a Hindu father and a Christian stepmother, should treat each relevant relative's share as a separate exercise under that relative's own applicable law rather than assuming one consistent rule governs the whole estate.

sections.heading: Where these disputes actually end up in court
paragraphs: In practice, few of these rules are argued in the abstract. They surface in a handful of recurring dispute patterns. One is a challenge to a mutation entry made in favour of only some of the legal heirs, typically sons, where daughters, a widow, or the children of a predeceased son were simply left off the revenue record, sometimes deliberately and sometimes through an official's own assumption about who counts as an heir. The correct remedy is a suit for declaration of title and, where the property is jointly held, partition, since the revenue authority making the mutation entry has no power to adjudicate a disputed inheritance claim.

A second recurring pattern involves a sale or gift executed by some heirs purporting to convey the entire property, without the knowledge or consent of a co-heir who was, for instance, living abroad, estranged from the family, or simply not consulted. Because an heir's share vests immediately on the intestate's death, such a transfer is valid only to the extent of the transferring heirs' own undivided shares; the excluded heir retains the right to seek partition and to have the property recovered or accounted for to the extent of their share, subject to the ordinary limitation rules governing suits for possession and partition.

A third pattern, increasingly common given how long some of these questions sat unsettled, involves heirs reopening a succession that was worked out years ago on legal advice that predated Vineeta Sharma or Arunachala Gounder. Whether such a claim can now succeed depends heavily on whether the earlier distribution was ever formalised through a registered partition deed or a court decree, since both decisions preserve the finality of partitions and settlements that were validly concluded before the relevant cutoff, while leaving open claims where no such final, formal step was ever taken and the property has simply continued to be held, informally, on the old and now-superseded assumption.

Limitation is the issue that most often decides whether a long-delayed claim by an excluded heir can still succeed. A suit for possession based on title, which is generally the right characterisation for a Class I heir seeking to recover their share from relatives or purchasers who have excluded them, is governed by Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, which allows twelve years running from the point the defendant's possession becomes adverse to the plaintiff's own right, not twelve years from the date of death itself. Because a co-heir's possession is ordinarily treated as possession on behalf of all the heirs rather than as adverse to them, the twelve-year clock frequently does not even begin to run until there is a clear, communicated act of exclusion, such as a sale to a stranger or an open denial of the claimant's share, which is one reason these disputes can resurface many years after a death that seemed, at the time, to have been quietly settled within the family.

sections.heading: A practical sequence for working out who gets what
paragraphs: A family facing an intestate estate for the first time is usually better served by working through a fixed sequence of questions than by jumping straight to dividing assets. The first question is whether the deceased left any document that could qualify as a valid will, even an informal one, since a will, if valid, displaces the entire intestate scheme described in this piece for whatever property it covers. The second is the classification question this piece opened with: for each significant asset, is it coparcenary property in an undivided Hindu family, or is it separate property the deceased built up independently, since the two tracks can produce materially different outcomes for the same relatives.

The third question is who the Class I heirs actually are, traced carefully through any predeceased children and their own children, since a family's informal understanding of "the children" sometimes omits a predeceased sibling's branch entirely, whether through oversight or through an old family estrangement that has nothing to do with the legal entitlement involved. Only once that list is settled does it make sense to move to documentation, deciding whether a legal heir certificate, a succession certificate, or both will actually be needed for the specific assets involved, bank balances and demat holdings usually calling for a succession certificate, while a ration card transfer or a small pension typically needs only a legal heir certificate.

Where every heir agrees on the division, a registered family settlement or partition deed, executed by all adult heirs, is generally the most durable way to record that agreement and to give a later purchaser or lender confidence that the title is clean, precisely because Vineeta Sharma and the ordinary law of partition both treat a validly executed, registered settlement as closing off the kind of reopening that an unrecorded, purely verbal family understanding cannot reliably prevent. Where even one heir disagrees, whether about the classification of an asset, the existence of a will, or the identity of the heirs themselves, the dispute belongs before a civil court for a declaration and, if the property cannot be sensibly divided, partition, rather than being left to an informal arrangement that a dissenting heir, or that heir's own children years later, remains free to challenge.

conclusion: Intestate succession under Hindu law rewards precision about two things families often treat as obvious when they are not: what kind of property is actually being divided, and what document is actually needed for what purpose. Getting the coparcenary-versus-separate-property distinction right decides which set of rules even applies, and getting Vineeta Sharma and Arunachala Gounder's holdings right decides whether a daughter's claim, long assumed to be weaker or time-barred, in fact survives.

A mutation entry, a legal heir certificate and a succession certificate solve three different problems for three different audiences, a revenue office, a range of administrative counters, and a bank or depository respectively, and none of them substitutes for a civil court's finding on a genuinely contested question of title. Where an estate's history includes an old death, an incomplete partition, or heirs who were never formally accounted for, the safer course is to have that history checked against the current law before relying on documents or assumptions that may predate it.

faqs.q: Does a daughter get an equal share with her brothers in her father's property if he died without a will?
faqs.a: Generally yes, whether the property was his separate property, governed by Section 8, or his interest in coparcenary property, governed by Section 6 as amended in 2005 and clarified in Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma (2020) 9 SCC 1. A daughter is a Class I heir under Section 8 on the same footing as a son, and she is also a coparcener by birth, so she shares in coparcenary property on the same terms as a son, regardless of whether she was born, or her father died, before or after the 2005 amendment, subject to the partition already having been finally concluded before 20 December 2004.

faqs.q: What is the difference between ancestral property and self-acquired property, and why does it matter?
faqs.a: Ancestral or coparcenary property is property in which a coparcener acquires an interest by birth, typically undivided family property passed down without partition. Self-acquired property is property a person built up independently, through earnings, a business, or a purchase unconnected to joint family funds. The distinction matters because the two categories historically followed different rules, survivorship for coparcenary property before 2005, inheritance under Section 8 for self-acquired property, and because Arunachala Gounder v Ponnusamy confirmed that even old, pre-1956 self-acquired property passes by inheritance to a daughter rather than by survivorship to male relatives.

faqs.q: What did Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma actually change?
faqs.a: It settled that the 2005 amendment making daughters coparceners applies to every living daughter regardless of her date of birth, and regardless of whether her father died before or after the amendment, because coparcenary status is acquired at birth rather than by a later event. It overruled Prakash v Phulavati and Mangammal v T.B. Raju, which had required the father to be alive on 9 September 2005 for the amendment to help his daughter. The one limit the Court preserved is that a partition finally and formally concluded, by registered deed or court decree, before 20 December 2004 is not reopened by this ruling.

faqs.q: If a man died before the Hindu Succession Act even existed, can his daughter still claim a share of his property today?
faqs.a: For his self-acquired property, yes, on the authority of Arunachala Gounder (Dead) by LRs v Ponnusamy (decided 20 January 2022), which held that self-acquired property has never passed by survivorship under Hindu law, even under the pre-1956 Mitakshara position, and instead devolves by inheritance to the deceased's heirs, including a sole surviving daughter, who takes it absolutely. Coparcenary property raises a separate analysis under Section 6 as clarified in Vineeta Sharma.

faqs.q: Is a legal heir certificate the same as a succession certificate?
faqs.a: No. A legal heir certificate is issued by a revenue authority such as a Tehsildar and is used mainly for local administrative purposes like transferring a ration card or small benefits; its procedure and recognition vary by state. A succession certificate is issued by a District Judge under the Indian Succession Act, 1925, following a petition under Section 372, and it is what banks and financial institutions typically require before releasing a deceased person's debts and securities. Neither document, by itself, proves title to immovable property.

faqs.q: Does mutation of a property into an heir's name prove that heir owns it?
faqs.a: No. Mutation is an entry in revenue or municipal records, used mainly to identify who is liable for property tax and who the local authority deals with administratively. Courts have consistently held that mutation does not create or extinguish title, and that a genuinely disputed question of inheritance has to be resolved through a civil suit for declaration, and partition where relevant, rather than through a revenue officer's mutation order.

faqs.q: What happens if a woman dies intestate without children, leaving property she inherited from her parents?
faqs.a: Section 15(2)(a) of the Hindu Succession Act pulls that specific property back to the heirs of her father, rather than letting it pass down the general order in Section 15(1) that would otherwise apply, for instance to her husband. This source-based exception applies only where she has no surviving son, daughter or child of a predeceased child; property she inherited from her husband is similarly pulled back to his heirs under Section 15(2)(b), while property she acquired herself is not subject to either exception.

faqs.q: Do Muslim and Christian families in India follow the same intestate succession rules as Hindu families?
faqs.a: No. Muslim personal law applies fixed shares to specified relatives rather than the Hindu scheme of Class I and Class II heirs, with Sunni and Shia law differing on some points, and a spouse, children and parents typically take simultaneously in fixed fractions rather than one class excluding another. Christians and Parsis are governed by separate intestate succession provisions within the Indian Succession Act, 1925, distinct from both the Hindu and the Muslim schemes. A family with relatives governed by different personal laws needs each relative's share worked out under that relative's own applicable law.
